To address these challenges, we propose ConsisX, a novel VLA framework that integrates cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency thinking in 3D for physically consistent robotic manipulation. Specifically, Cross-View Association Modeling (CAM) is proposed to introduce cross-view spatial proximity constraints in a shared 3D space to reduce cross-view incorrect association. Entity Coherence Organization (ECO) is designed to organize cross-view local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, thereby addressing cross-view information fragmentation. Consistent Action Conditioning (CAC) is introduced to condition action prediction on task-relevant 3D entity evidence for cross-view consistent action execution. Experiments on 3 real-world manipulation tasks and 4 simulation benchmarks establish ConsisX as an effective and competitive framework for robotic manipulation.

title: Robust Lateral String Stability and Error Attenuation for Heterogeneous Vehicle Platoons
authors: Sixu Li, Swaroop Darbha, Yang Zhou
publish: arXiv
abstract: Keeping an entire vehicle platoon close to its planned path is essential for navigating road boundaries and obstacles safely. Followers may rely on predecessor information for lateral guidance, which couples their lateral dynamics and allows errors to propagate downstream. This paper develops a robust lateral string stability framework to study this propagation and achieve downstream error attenuation in heterogeneous platoons under varying longitudinal motion and local perturbations. Arc-length-based feedback linearization gives each vehicle the same nominal lateral error dynamics, with parameter uncertainty and external disturbances represented as local perturbations. We define robust $\mathcal L_2$ lateral string stability in terms of platoon-length-uniform error bounds and derive a sufficient condition for achieving it. Furthermore, we show that the same condition guarantees platoon-length-uniform $\mathcal L_\infty$ error bounds. For the considered control formulations, predecessor tracking (PT) can accumulate lateral errors, whereas desired-path tracking (DT) prevents this accumulation. We propose a learn-from-predecessor (LFP) strategy with explicit gains for downstream error attenuation and characterize how intervehicle perturbation differences limit this attenuation. Simulations validate the theoretical findings under vehicle heterogeneity, varying longitudinal motion, and local perturbations.

title: Spatial dimensionality affects the convective thawing of permafrost
authors: M. Magnani, S. Musacchio, G. Boffetta
publish: arXiv
abstract: Permafrost thaw is one of the major consequences of ongoing climate change, with potentially far-reaching implications for high-latitude and high-altitude environments. Because permafrost degradation is a subsurface phenomenon, its dynamics and future evolution are primarily investigated through numerical models. Yet, the role of groundwater convection in permafrost thawing is an underrepresented process. Here, we explore how the spatial dimensionality affects the simulation of permafrost thaw and heat transport within the thawed layer, known as the active layer. Using two- and three-dimensional (2D and 3D) simulations, with realistic parameter sets that enable convection, we show that permafrost thawing rate and heat transport are systematically slower in 2D than in 3D simulations. The ice-water interface develops spatial patterns that coincides with the underlying convective structures, with rising cold plumes and descending warm plumes shaping its morphology. These findings reveal a coupling between convective flow structures and the evolving geometry of the permafrost boundary, and highlight the importance of three-dimensional representations of subsurface heat transport for accurately capturing permafrost thaw dynamics in land-surface models.

title: Impact of structured noise on bosonic quantum error correction
authors: Guoyu Shu, Ling Hu, Hongbo Wu, Zhongchu Ni, Yanyan Cai, Xiaowei Deng, Pan Zheng, Pengbo Li, Fei Yan, Song Liu, Dapeng Yu, Yuan Xu
publish: arXiv
abstract: Bosonic quantum error correction relies on an accurate description of single-photon loss dissipation using an ideal annihilation operator, under which correctable loss errors act equivalently on different logical code states. In realistic weakly nonlinear bosonic modes, however, coupling to a structured environment can render photon loss Fock-state dependent, thereby modifying the effective dissipation operator and deforming the associated error space. Here, we experimentally investigate this effect in a three-dimensional circuit quantum electrodynamics system. By injecting spectrally engineered environmental noise into a weakly nonlinear oscillator, we observe pronounced frequency selectivity in the measured Fock-state dynamics. While the long-time transition rates converge to the Markovian limit, the transient dynamics display distinctly non-Markovian behavior, in quantitative agreement with a second-order time-convolutionless theory. By applying narrowband noise to a binomially encoded logical qubit, we further demonstrate Fock-state-dependent dissipation channels that drive logical states beyond the nominally correctable error space. These results establish structured environmental noise as a mechanism for deforming photon-loss errors in weakly nonlinear bosonic systems and highlight the need to incorporate realistic, state-dependent dissipation into the design and characterization of bosonic quantum error correction.

title: Anatomy of orbital and spin responses in GaAs and Si: Hall, inverse Faraday, and magneto-optical Kerr effects
authors: Sanaz Alikhah, Daegeun Jo, Peter M. Oppeneer
publish: arXiv
abstract: Magneto-optical signals in nonmagnetic semiconductors entangle spin and orbital contributions, both in angular-momentum generation and magneto-optical detection. We calculate these contributions for electron-doped GaAs and Si using density-functional theory, linear-response theory, and a second-order density-matrix treatment of the inverse Faraday effect. At small electron doping, the intrinsic orbital Hall conductivity exceeds its spin counterpart in magnitude, while the orbital contribution to light-induced magnetization dominates over broad photon-energy ranges. We show that orbital- and spin-resolved optical Hall and polar Kerr coefficients exhibit stronger sensitivity to orbital moments than to equal spin moments. This contrast reflects direct electric-dipole coupling to orbital motion versus spin-orbit-mediated coupling to spin polarization. Consequently, Si maintains a substantial orbital magneto-optical response despite its weak spin-orbit interaction. At probe energies of 1.5 eV in GaAs and 3.0 eV in Si, the magnitude of the Kerr rotation per unit orbital moment is approximately 5 and 13 times larger than that per unit spin moment, respectively. Combining the calculated Hall conductivities and Kerr coefficients with a phenomenological drift-diffusion model yields predominantly orbital edge signals for the assumed diffusion constants and relaxation lengths. These results indicate that optical detection of induced magnetization in doped semiconductors such as GaAs and Si can be dominated by orbital signals, and therefore cannot be interpreted solely in terms of spin polarization.

title: Periodic orbit asymptotics and dynamical zeta functions for smooth surface diffeomorphisms
authors: Gang Liao, Yao Tong
publish: arXiv
abstract: Let $f$ be a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism of a closed surface $M$, and let $H$ be a closed homoclinic class with topological entropy $h=h_{\mathrm{top}}(f|H)>0$ and homoclinic period $\ell$. We prove that \[ \forall\,0<χ<h,\qquad \lim_{\ell\mid n,\;n\to\infty} \frac{\#\mathrm{Per}_χ(n,H)}{e^{nh}}=\ell, \] where $\mathrm{Per}_χ(n,H)$ denotes the saddle points in $H$ of least period $n$ whose Lyapunov exponents lie outside $[-χ,χ]$. We also prove exponential remainders for the class and global counting formulas. As a result, for every $0<χ<h_{\mathrm{top}}(f)$, the Artin--Mazur zeta function of all $χ$-hyperbolic periodic orbits, including sinks and sources, extends meromorphically beyond its disk of convergence. Its leading poles are determined by the periods of the ergodic maximal measures. This answers the meromorphic continuation question of Buzzi.

title: MirrorGuard: Defending LiDAR Perception against Passive Mirror Attacks
authors: Aymen Bouferroum, Ildi Alla, Selma Yahia, Vincent Lenders, Valeria Loscri
publish: arXiv
abstract: Mirror-based LiDAR attacks passively redirect automotive LiDAR's beams to create phantom objects in the vehicle perception. Recent work has demonstrated that these attacks may cause vehicles to brake for a phantom where nothing stands. Every phantom return is a genuine time-of-flight measurement, so current spoofing defenses are not able to differentiate phantoms from real objects. We present MirrorGuard, a physics-informed defense that identifies and removes mirror-induced phantom returns before they affect downstream perception. MirrorGuard tests three consequences of the reflected path. Every phantom bearing crosses the mirror's finite aperture, its opaque surface blocks any direct return beyond it, and the two reflections off the mirror dim the phantom. MirrorGuard identifies a phantom by these cues over multiple scans and removes the reflected beams before it reaches any detector or occupancy grid. On real-world recordings of this attack, MirrorGuard removes 96.31% of the phantom's returns at 98.30% precision, with 99.99% of non-phantom returns untouched. In a closed loop with the CARLA driving simulator and the open-source stack (Autoware), a vehicle without the defense halts for an obstacle that is not present and a following car crashes into its rear. With MirrorGuard, no vehicle produces a halt or a crash. MirrorGuard runs at 59 ms mean per scan on a CPU and is a software-only solution that does not require new hardware or environmental training.

title: MMMem: Self-Improving Agents with Task-Aware Multimodal Experience Consolidation
authors: Yuxuan Chen, Changwei Lv, Yunfei Li, Zhongjing Du, Kehui Tan, Zijun Liao, Ruochong Zheng, Hao Chen, Can Deng, Zheni Zeng, Chang Liu, Jie Chen
publish: arXiv
abstract: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.

title: Interpreting the $γ$-Ray Emission of the Cygnus X region with a Combined Cygnus OB2 and Cygnus X-3 Scenario
authors: Caijin Xie, Zhihao Ouyang, Yudong Cui, Lili Yang
publish: arXiv
abstract: The recent detection of high-energy $γ$-ray emission up to PeV energies from the Cygnus X region points to the presence of a PeVatron therein. This region hosts notable candidates such as the Cygnus OB2 association, which may be associated with PeV $γ$-photons detected by the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO). The X-ray binary Cygnus X-3 also lies along the line of sight to the Cygnus X region, and LHAASO has observed modulated PeV $γ$-ray flux from its direction, indicating that its contribution is also non-negligible. Here, we attempt to interpret the $γ$-ray emission of the Cygnus X region using a combined scenario. Assuming a hadronic origin, we consider contributions from Cygnus OB2, Cygnus X-3, and Galactic cosmic rays (GCRs). Our results show that Cygnus OB2 alone, or its combination with the GCR component, is insufficient to account for the multiwavelength observations, whereas including the $γ$-ray emission from Cygnus X-3 naturally explains these observations. This suggests that the $γ$-ray emission from the Cygnus X region has a more complex origin, necessitating a joint consideration of Cygnus OB2 and Cygnus X-3. The expected neutrino flux from hadronic interactions extends into the GeV band and can help reveal the radiation mechanism of Cygnus X-3, underscoring the need for high-sensitivity GeV neutrino observatories.

title: OpenAI's proof of the local smoothing conjecture: A harmonic analytic perspective
authors: Xiangyu Wang
publish: arXiv
abstract: This note presents OpenAI's proof of the local smoothing conjecture. It is written for harmonic analysts who may be new to quaternionic Monge--Ampère equations. We introduce the quaternionic Hessian and explain how the associated determinant equation leads to the critical annular estimate.

title: A response-based self-energy from equation-of-motion coupled-cluster theory and its reduction to GW, GW+SOSEX, and GF2
authors: Ajith Perera, Pierre-François Loos
publish: arXiv
abstract: We construct a frequency-dependent one-particle correlation self-energy by coupling a reference Green's function to the neutral excitation response obtained from equation-of-motion coupled-cluster theory with singles and doubles (EOM-CCSD). Direct, mixed direct-antisymmetrized, and fully antisymmetrized choices of the external interaction vertices define three approximations, all admitting an explicit spectral representation without numerical frequency integration. In the bare-state limit, the mixed and fully antisymmetrized forms recover second-order Green's-function theory (GF2), whereas the direct form retains only its ring contribution. With a direct random-phase approximation (RPA) response, the direct and mixed forms reduce to $G_0W_0$ and $G_0W_0$ plus second-order screened exchange (SOSEX), respectively. For molecular ionization potentials, replacing the RPA response by EOM-CCSD generally lowers the ionization energies, whereas introducing exchange at one external vertex raises them. These substantial opposing effects partially compensate, although the mixed approximation does not systematically improve upon conventional $G_0W_0$, either against IP-EOM-CCSD or QUESTDB reference energies (aug-cc-pVDZ mean absolute errors relative to the QUESTDB theoretical best estimates: 0.45 vs 0.36~eV). A third-order perturbative analysis reveals that the three approximations retain different contributions and weights of particle-hole diagrams while omitting explicit particle-particle and hole-hole ladder contributions and the static self-energy. In particular, the fully antisymmetrized form recovers GF2 at second order but assigns incorrect weights to its retained third-order diagrams. These findings highlight the importance of a balanced treatment of screening and vertex corrections in constructing accurate self-energy approximations.

title: Hypergraph Ramsey Numbers via Oriented Palette Constructions
authors: Hanzhi Bai, Xinyu Hu, Kaidi Liu, Guanghui Wang
publish: arXiv
abstract: Given a family $\mathcal F$ of $k$-graphs, the Ramsey number $r_k(\mathcal F,n)$ is the minimum $N$ such that every red/blue coloring of the edges of $K_N^{(k)}$ yields either a red copy of some $F\in\mathcal F$ or a blue copy of $K_n^{(k)}$. In particular, if $\mathcal F=\{F\}$, we write $r_k(F,n)$. In this paper, we use oriented palette constructions and the hypergraph container method to obtain a lower bound on $r_k(\mathcal F,n)$ for special families $\mathcal F$. More precisely, we independently label lower-dimensional faces and use the palette to exclude prescribed red configurations, while a container argument controls the size of blue cliques. As a first application of our theorem, we obtain \(r_k(B^{(k)},n)>2^{Ω_k(n\log n)}\). Combined with the upper bound due to Mubayi and Suk, this yields \(r_k(B^{(k)},n)=2^{Θ_k(n\log n)}\), where \(B^{(k)}\) is the half-graph. This answers in the affirmative a question posed by Mubayi and Suk. As a second application of our theorem, we show $r_k(k+1,3;n)=2^{Θ_k(n^{k-2}\log n)}$, which, together with a new stepping-up lemma developed in this paper, further yields $r_k(k+1,t;n)=\twr_{t-1}(Θ_{k,t}(n^{k-t+1}\log n))$ for every fixed $k\ge6$ and $4\le t\le k-2$, where $\twr_1(x)=x$ and $\twr_{j+1}(x)=2^{\twr_j(x)}$. Here $r_k(k+1,t;n)$ denotes the minimum $N$ such that every red/blue coloring of the $k$-subsets of an $N$-vertex set contains either $k+1$ vertices spanning at least $t$ red edges or a blue clique of order $n$. As a third application of our theorem, we show that $r_k(F_{\ell,k,d},n)>2^{Ω_{k,\ell,d}(n^{k-d-2}\log n)}$ for all fixed integers $k\ge4$, $1\le d\le k-3$, and $\ell\ge2k+1$ with $k\nmid\ell$, where $F_{\ell,k,d}$ is obtained from the $k$-uniform tight cycle of length $\ell$ by deleting $d$ consecutive edges.

title: SonicRender: Structured and Time-Grounded Rendering of Multi-Event Audio Scene Generation
authors: Yunrui Cai, Xu Li, Yan Rong, Dingdong Wang, Yucheng Zhou, Xixin Wu, Chen Zhang, Zhiyong Wu, Helen Meng
publish: arXiv
abstract: While unified audio generators can synthesize speech, music, and sound effects within a single model, producing a plausible mixture is only part of the challenge: a complex scene request also specifies which events occur, who produces them, and when they are heard. To satisfy these compositional constraints in a single generation pass, we present SonicRender, a unified multi-event audio renderer. Its Temporal Audio Scene Graph (TASG) binds persistent source identities to localized speech, music, ambience, and sound-effect events, together with their content, acoustic roles, relations, and timestamped windows. We further introduce AbsTime, which supplies the audio latent stream with absolute-frame coordinates and valid-canvas duration. Through joint text-audio attention and conditional flow matching, the renderer learns to realize structured, timed scenes as coherent mixtures. On the MMAG timestamp benchmark, SonicRender achieves speech/sound F1 scores of 0.79/0.60, exceeding the strongest reported scores in our comparison. On our SceneMix evaluation, it attains 85.4% all-event recall, 83.9% window-hit rate, and 95.7% speaker accuracy. Subjective study further demonstrates significant improvements over all five comparison systems in both perceived audio quality and scene realization. Results across speech, general audio, music, multi-event load, and temporal-grounding analyses establish precise, composition-aware audio rendering within a unified generator. Demo page: https://caiyunrui.github.io/SonicRender.

title: The Tate conjecture for abelian fourfolds
authors: Matt Broe, Ruofan Jiang
publish: arXiv
abstract: We prove the Tate conjecture for non-CM and non-ordinary abelian fourfolds over positive characteristic function fields. Combining our previous works (2512.00687 and 2608.28651), this establishes the Tate conjecture for abelian fourfolds over finitely generated fields. Along the way, we classify the $l$-adic monodromy of abelian fourfolds in characteristic $p$ via mixed characteristic lifts and methods from convergent and overconvergent crystalline monodromy, and show that Zarhin's minuscule weights conjecture holds for abelian varieties up to dimension 4. These enable us to prove a characteristic $p$ variant of the Mumford--Tate conjecture for most abelian fourfolds, and reduce the Tate conjecture to Markman's results on the Hodge conjecture.

title: Dynamical evolution and rheological behavior of a sheared compound vesicle with a highly viscous core: a mesoscale particle-based study
authors: A. Lamura
publish: arXiv
abstract: We study numerically the dynamics and the rheology of a two-dimensional compound vesicle in wall-bounded shear flow, as a minimal model of a nucleated cell. We consider the configuration in which the annular fluid is iso-viscous with the external one, while the inner core is more viscous. Increasing the core viscosity drives the external vesicle away from steady tank-treading at values $φ\geq 0.6$. When an internal body is present, the annular fluid partially shields the outer membrane from the viscous core, so that at small filling fractions the external vesicle retains tank-treading with a higher inclination angle and the intrinsic viscosity stays comparatively low. The internal vesicle, by contrast, tumbles and migrates away from the center, and at high $φ$ this motion couples back to the host, producing intermittent shape excursions of the external membrane. The inner viscous body thus acts as an internal governor of the dynamical state.

title: Accelerating interatomic potential development through student-driven exploration and reliability-aware distillation
authors: Ruiqi Dong, Haotian Huang, Yubin Hu, Guixiang Zeng
publish: arXiv
abstract: Conventional two-stage distillation first establishes a teacher through teacher-driven configuration exploration, a costly first stage for complex materials, and then uses its predictions to supervise students, potentially propagating teacher-label errors. Here, we propose distillation-driven teacher-student co-evolution (DICE), which uses a fast student to accelerate configuration exploration and replaces the fixed teacher-to-student sequence with alternating student and teacher updates. A representation-based support-assessment algorithm routes high-support configurations to teacher labelling and selects low-support configurations for density functional theory (DFT) calculations to update the teacher, thereby reducing the risk of teacher-label error propagation to students. Across Al2O3 (structural ceramics), yttria-stabilised zirconia (solid electrolytes) and MIL-120(Al) (a metal-organic framework), DICE develops reliable compact potentials using only 140-494 target DFT reference configurations per system; total recorded student exploration times per system are just 2.6-5.1% of the corresponding teacher-driven estimates. Combining computational efficiency with broad applicability across diverse material systems, DICE provides a practical route to developing reliable compact interatomic potentials.

title: Coulomb-Induced $K^- pp$ Molecular State
authors: T. Massimino, Z. Papp, J. Revai, J. -M. Richard, N. V. Shevchenko
publish: arXiv
abstract: We studied a new bound state in the three-body system consisting of an antikaon and two nucleons. The state is primarily induced by the Coulomb interactions between the $K^-$ and the two protons, and is modified by the strong $K^- p$ and $pp$ interactions. This spatially extended molecular state has binding energy and width that are of the order of keV, compared to the tens of MeV binding energy and width of the famous quasi-bound $K^- pp$ state caused primarily by the strong interaction.

title: Reciprocal Range-Doppler Estimation with Partial Path Association for Asynchronous Bistatic OFDM-ISAC
authors: Jiayao Shao, Zhendong Li, Wenjie Wang, Zhou Su, Kaitao Meng, Wen Chen
publish: arXiv
abstract: In bistatic integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), clock asynchronism shifts the delay and Doppler measured from orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) echoes. The two stations may see different reflectors, so the receiver must identify which echoes belong to the same path before combining the two views. For partial path association, PreVote finds a common displacement in the directional delay and Doppler differences. One-to-one assignment at this displacement accepts compatible pairs and allows other paths to remain unmatched. Each station uses coherent compression to form a subcarrier vector and a slow-time vector per path. For range-Doppler estimation in reciprocal sensing, the center multiplies paired vectors without conjugation. The opposite constant clock terms cancel, and a correct pair yields twice the physical phase slopes of one path. A Cramer-Rao bound (CRB) for fixed identities and phase branches quantifies the shared clock uncertainty. At the higher signal-to-noise ratios tested, reciprocal fusion yields lower range and Doppler errors than both receivers using calibrated echoes. Under partial visibility, displacement-based matching recovers more targets with correct identities and prescribed accuracy than separate centering with the same fusion stage. Balancing directional energy and extending the common aperture improve Doppler accuracy, while carrier frequency variation increases error.

title: Numerical simulations of CCP-2D GEC with sGMRES
authors: Zhenyu Zou, Haoran Guan, Kangxin Liu, Yufeng Wei, Yipei Chen, Peiting You, Yuwei Fan
publish: arXiv
abstract: Fluid models provide an efficient means of simulating the low-temperature gas discharges, which are important in semiconductor manufacturing. This work presents, to the best of our knowledge, the first systematic numerical framework for the Gaseous Electronics Conference (GEC) reference cell of the 2D capacitively coupled plasma (CCP). The framework employs a structured, nonuniform cylindrical mesh to resolve the spatial gradients. A semi-implicit Scharfetter-Gummel (SG) scheme is used for the Poisson's equation, while the implicit SG schemes are applied to the continuity equations and the electron energy equation. Both the explicit and and the implicit formulations based on the conventional drift-diffusion terms are also investigated. To solve the resulting large-scale linear systems, we introduce an incomplete LU (ILU)-preconditioned sketched GMRES (sGMRES) method as the solver. As far as we know, this work is the first to apply the randomized sGMRES to the practical simulations in the engineering. By reducing the cost of the global orthogonalization, ILU-sGMRES achieves greater computational efficiency than ILU-GMRES while maintaining the accuracy, particularly at relatively large values of the restart. Specifically, numerical tests demonstrate that ILU-sGMRES can reduce the end-to-end wall-clock time by up to 25.38\% on a single machine and up to 11.71\% in a three-node benchmark compared with the conventional ILU-GMRES, while maintaining a maximum relative difference across plasma fields of only 0.194\%. Numerical experiments compare the performance of different numerical schemes and solvers, demonstrating the robustness of ILU-sGMRES in the real simulation.

title: RoboAda: Adapting Frozen Robot Policies at Test Time to Physics They Cannot See
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Zijian Jin, Shuaicheng Niu, Baian Chen, Weirui Ye, Jihun Hamm, Yilun Du
publish: arXiv
abstract: Pretrained robot policies decide what to do from camera images, yet some of the physics that decides whether their plans succeed is not visible. An object may look light but be 100 times heavier, and a weakened joint or a lagging controller leaves no trace in the image. When the physics at deployment differs from training, the plan is often still right but is executed as if nothing had changed. Training on such variations in advance cannot handle unseen changes, while adapting once deployed either changes the plan, leaving the miscalibrated commands in place, or updates a robot model by gradient steps that do not know how reliable they are and can make the robot worse even when nothing has changed. We propose RoboAda, which keeps the policy and its plan unchanged and corrects the commands that carry it out by inferring at test time how the robot turns commands into motion. The key observation is that the robot's own motion reveals the change: after each action chunk, an inverse-dynamics model of the original robot converts the observed motion into the commands it would have needed, yielding free labels at every step. Competing hypotheses of how the robot responds, including that nothing has changed, are weighted by how well they predict these labels, and the next chunk is sent with the commands that best realize the plan under them. RoboAda needs no reward, no gradient step and no data from the changed robot. We evaluate RoboAda with five frozen policies on LIBERO, two world action models and three vision-language-action models. Under eleven physical shifts, it more than doubles their average success, from 27.8% to 62.9%. It beats the best of seven test-time adaptation methods by 17.3 points on Cosmos Policy, and largely preserves the policies' success when nothing has changed. On bimanual RoboTwin 2.0 in joint space, it raises success under joint-target offsets from 24.9% to 78.8%.

title: Counterfactual Velocity Steering for World Action Models
authors: Xufeng Zhan, Yuanzhi Liang, Ye Lu, Haibin Huang, Chi Zhang, Xuelong Li
publish: arXiv
abstract: Flow-based robot policies generate actions by repeatedly evaluating a conditional velocity field, so test-time bias correction seems simple: query the action expert under a task-agnostic condition and subtract that velocity from the task-conditioned prediction. We show this is often wrong. On Fast-WAM across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, mean-instruction predictions align strongly with task-conditioned velocities (cosine approximately 0.94-0.95). Averaging eight completed-state references barely cancels this direction: their mean norm is 98.3% of the mean individual norm. References thus contain a large shared transport component, not only harmful bias, and aggressive subtraction damages generation. We propose a same-state diagnostic and shrinkage analysis showing that the optimal correction scale depends on reference signal-to-noise. This motivates geometry-calibrated action debiasing, which removes only the component orthogonal to the task velocity and predicts a small task-dependent scale from instruction geometry. In controlled RoboTwin experiments, corrupting instructions still permits 25.1% success (50 tasks, 20 episodes), whereas dynamic visual corruption nearly eliminates success. A fixed centered orthogonal correction reaches 92.7% versus a 92.1% baseline in one randomized 1000-trial sweep, but gains are non-monotonic and within run-to-run variation. An angular scale pilot has an offline oracle-gated bound of 94.5%; its best learned online realization reaches 92.5%. These results identify shared flow and train-serve mismatch as central obstacles and provide a reproducible foundation for conditional correction.

title: ToWo-VTON: Take-Off Wear-On Virtual Try-On via Topology-aware Decoupling
authors: Zhenchen Wan, Tianxi Chen, Runqi Lin, Tianyi Bo, Ce Chen, Jiaxin Huang, Yanwu Xu, Tongliang Liu, Mingming Gong
publish: arXiv
abstract: Virtual Try-On (VTON) aims to synthesize garment transfer without physical trials. Although recent methods perform well on upper-body garments, they still struggle in lower-body and full-body scenarios with complex occlusions and large silhouette changes. To address this limitation, we introduce ToWo (Take-Off Wear-On), a two-stage paradigm that decouples body structure estimation from garment synthesis. Take-Off first generates a tight-fitting body proxy that provides estimated structural guidance, and Wear-On then synthesizes the target garment conditioned on this prior. This decoupling reduces source-garment interference, supporting garment placement under substantial silhouette variations. Built on this paradigm, we propose ToWo-VTON, a unified topology-aware framework with structure-aware supervision. We construct the Body-Fitting DressCode (BFDC) dataset via body-aware diffusion and VLM-based filtering to provide body-proxy supervision across upper-, lower-, and full-body cases. We instantiate ToWo-VTON on both diffusion-based and MLLM-guided backbones. For diffusion-based models, we fine-tune on BFDC using the body proxy as the person input. For the MLLM-guided model, we use native backbone conditioning for the body proxy and target garment, and add Garment Boosting Attention (GBA) to preserve garment details. Experiments on VITON-HD and DressCode demonstrate improvements over the evaluated baselines, with KID reductions of 26.1% and 58.6% for diffusion-based and MLLM-guided implementations, respectively. The combined BFDC-training and Take-Off/Wear-On strategy also produces more coherent limb layouts and garment boundaries across the evaluated garment categories.

title: Remotest Operator Control String-Averaging Methods in Feasibility-Seeking
authors: Yair Censor, Ariel Nisenbaum, Simeon Reich
publish: arXiv
abstract: The string-averaging (SA) method is a versatile algorithmic scheme for solving feasibility-seeking problems. It partitions the index set of all constraints into subsets of indices, called strings, allowing the user to apply operators successively along each string separately, and thus in parallel. The end-points of all such string operations are convexly combined to create the next iterate. Due to its flexible framework, SA is not restricted solely to this procedure; however, this characteristic applies only to the simultaneous step, while the sequential one is restricted to operator compositions. To permit alternative strategies in the latter, a novel algorithmic structure termed the Skeletal SA is introduced. Although its convergence is not established, it serves as a foundational "parent" structure that unveils unexamined SA algorithmic structures, as well as other known methods, obscured by standard compositions. To demonstrate the benefit of adopting the Skeletal SA framework over the standard SA scheme, we investigate a new approach, where instead of passing sequentially over each string via compositions, we employ a remotest-set-control-like strategy on every string by identifying the index of the operator farthest from the current iterate, and invoking it. This method favorably handles the common fixed point problem (CFPP), which requires finding a point within the intersection of finitely many constraint sets whose intersection is nonempty. Many iterative methods, including SA ones, have been proposed to solve the CFPP due to its importance in many scientific fields. However, remotest operator control SA (ROC-SA) methods have remained unexamined in this context.

title: Making Protocol Effects Explicit: LLM-to-Packet Simulation for Superpod Interconnect Exploration
authors: Yu Zhu, Xinhao Yang, Zhaoshi Li, Baodong Wu, Boxun Li, Wenxue Li, Guohao Dai, Hongyang Jia, Shuwen Deng, Huazhong Yang, Yuan Xie, Zhenhua Zhu, Yu Wang
publish: arXiv
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become the foundation of modern AI services. The rapid growth of LLM sizes and context lengths has exceeded the memory capacity of a single GPU or NPU, requiring model partitioning across devices. However, partitioning models across devices introduces costly communication overhead, driving the need for superpods with large-scale, high-bandwidth, low-latency scale-up fabrics. Exploring superpod designs requires accurate interconnect simulation, as communication latency is jointly determined by link technologies, topologies, and scale-up protocol-stack choices. Latency-bandwidth models estimate communication latency using a startup term and a transfer term derived from message size and effective bandwidth. But they fail to capture contention and protocol effects. Packet-level simulators like ns-3 model routing, queueing, and packet timing, but require protocol-specific LLM-to-packet implementations. This paper presents ProtoBridge, an ns-3-based LLM-to-packet simulator for superpod interconnect exploration. To make protocol effects explicit, ProtoBridge introduces two abstraction layers over ns-3: (1) an operation-to-packet (OTP) layer that captures protocol-specific packet exchanges and dependencies, and (2) a packet-execution (PEX) layer that applies shared packet-level mechanisms to the ns-3 event system. ProtoBridge achieves average latency error of 17.8\% on H200 NVLink4 and 10.3\% on C500 MetaXLink. To enable faster superpod evaluation for further interconnect exploration, we derive a surrogate model that combines OTP parameters with analytical models of PEX mechanisms. The surrogate reduces evaluation time from 2.38$\sim$75.70s to 20.5us per operation. We use ProtoBridge to analyze two emerging superpod designs, scale-up memory pool and co-packaged optics (CPO) interconnects, revealing design insights for future LLM superpod architectures.

title: Quantum simulation of low-temperature impurity models
authors: Jiaqing Jiang, Nathan Ju
publish: arXiv
abstract: Quantum impurity models, which describe a small but strongly-interacting subsystem coupled to a large noninteracting bath, are the computational core of dynamical mean field theory and play an important role in simulating strongly correlated materials. We develop quantum algorithms for efficiently simulating these models at low temperatures and with high precision. For any impurity model on $n$ fermionic modes with fixed impurity size: (1) We give a quantum algorithm that prepares the thermal state at inverse temperature $β$ to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. This algorithm is the first to achieve both polynomial scaling in the inverse temperature and polylogarithmic scaling in the precision. When the Hamiltonian has an inverse-polynomial spectral gap, our quantum algorithm prepares its ground state to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log(1/δ))$. (2) We further give a quantum algorithm that prepares a purification of the thermal state in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. Using this purification, we estimate static and dynamical properties with error $δ$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $β$ and linear in $1/δ$ up to polylogarithmic factors, achieving the Heisenberg scaling. Our algorithms build on quantum Gibbs samplers, which are quantum analogues of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. By using global jump operators instead of local ones, we avoid the $\exp(β)$ overhead commonly associated with quantum Gibbs samplers, making them efficient for impurity models even at low temperatures.

title: PCC: Pivotal Channel Compensation for Layer Pruning of Large Language Models
authors: Xiangqian Wang, Yucheng Zhang, Zhaohong Jia, Kun Jing, Chunchun Li
publish: arXiv
abstract: Treating independent layers as the minimal pruning unit allows layer pruning to efficiently eliminate many redundant parameters and achieve high compression rates. Layer pruning has become a promising and prevalent structured pruning technique for large language models (LLMs). However, multi-layer removal can lead to significant performance degradation for LLMs. Although some works have explored various compensation methods for pruned layers, they are inefficient and costly. Observing that the expression of a large proportion of information is concentrated on a small number of pivotal channels, we propose a novel post-pruning compensation method for layer pruning, called pivotal channel compensation (PCC). PCC can achieve significant performance improvement by compensating for a small number of channels through learnable linear transformations at the pruning interface. Besides, we propose a new evaluation metric, called channel-wise average performance improvement (CAPI), which can measure the efficiency of channel-wise compensation. Our experimental results across various LLMs demonstrate that PCC can achieve significant and consistent improvements and high CAPI on language modeling and zero-shot question answering for the state-of-the-art cross-layer and consecutive-layer pruning methods. Compared with existing compensation methods, PCC can achieve competitive results with fewer additional parameters and less training cost.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation in the Agentic Era: Tradition, Present, and Prospect
authors: Chenming Tang, Haolin Li, Yiran Li, Zixian Yang, Lizhu Zhai, Rui Sun, Qizhou Huang, Yunfang Wu
publish: arXiv
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) couples frozen language models with external, updatable knowledge, so that generation is grounded in retrieved evidence rather than in parametric memory alone. This work maps RAG in the agentic era by joining them on a single lifecycle axis, from offline indexing through pre-retrieval, retrieval, post-retrieval, and orchestration over these stages. It treats indexing and orchestration as first-class components and agentic workflows as a paradigm of their own, and it covers the agentic work that has appeared since those reviews. Beyond these components, it covers evaluation, applications, and the questions that remain open for future exploration. From tradition to present and beyond, this work systematically reviews RAG from a perspective of the agentic era.

title: Observable-Level Expressivity in Fixed-Readout Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Iqra Bashir, Yuanfeng Wang, Mingda Huang, Keren Li, Qi Qin
publish: arXiv
abstract: A central question in quantum machine learning is which functions of an input state a model can represent when its measurement is fixed by hardware or by experimental design. We address this question for quantum neural networks with a fixed readout observable, where the trainable pre-measurement dynamics determine the effective observable in the Heisenberg picture and the scalar output is the measured expectation value itself, without trainable affine post-processing. We characterize the reachable effective observables under three physical resource classes: unitary evolution, which preserves the spectrum of the readout; mixed-unitary evolution, which relaxes this to a majorization constraint while preserving the trace; and completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) evolution, whose Heisenberg adjoint is unital rather than trace-preserving and therefore lifts the trace constraint inherited at the mixed-unitary level. The three reachable sets are a fixed-spectrum orbit, its convex hull, and an operator interval, and the inclusions are strict for any readout that is not proportional to the identity. The separation is witnessed locally: for a fixed Pauli readout $Z_j$ on an arbitrary number of qubits, the amplitude-damping observable $γ\id+(1-γ)Z_j$ lies outside the mixed-unitary level for every $γ>0$. We realize the CPTP level with a Stinespring-channelized circuit and derive closed-form loss floors, $4γ^2/3$ and $γ^2$ for the unitary and mixed-unitary levels and zero at the CPTP level, which the numerics reproduce within precision. Structured-observable, Rényi-moment and classification experiments illustrate how the hierarchy manifests in finite-depth ansätze. The results identify which spectral constraint each physical resource relaxes, framing reachable-observable classes as a resource for expressivity rather than an architectural advantage.

title: WaDiS: Boundary-Preserving Diffusion Segmentation via Multi-Scale Wavelet Conditioning and Frequency-Aware Gating
authors: Qiang Gao, Yi Wang, Yong Zhang, Bin Fang, Yong Li, Lan Du, Cunjian Chen
publish: arXiv
abstract: Diffusion models have shown strong potential in medical image segmentation due to their generative capabilities and robustness. However, existing methods often struggle to preserve fine anatomical boundaries and to retain multi-scale structural information due to the loss of spatial and frequency details during feature encoding, particularly in complex clinical imaging conditions. This work presents WaDiS, a wavelet-powered conditional latent diffusion framework for medical image segmentation that addresses these limitations through multi-scale wavelet conditioning and frequency-aware information filtering for boundary preservation. The model adopts a multi-scale wavelet conditioning encoder to retain rich structural features, leveraging its lossless nature to better preserve semantic priors critical to the diffusion process. In addition, a Frequency-Aware Gating Block (FAGB) is introduced into the skip connections of the diffusion U-Net, enabling adaptive spectral filtering and residual fusion to better emphasize boundary structures while reducing irrelevant content. To improve generalization across clinical domains, we adopt a structure-preserving color augmentation strategy during training. Specifically, global color statistics are transferred between samples in the LAB color space, allowing the model to decouple appearance from structure and focus more on anatomical shape rather than color bias. Experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that WaDiS consistently outperforms existing diffusion-based and conventional segmentation methods, with notable improvements in boundary accuracy, robustness to noise, and generalization under color variation. The code for this work will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

title: AdaptRouter: Adaptive Routing across Evolving Tasks and Models
authors: Jingpu Yang, Fengxian Ji, Tianhao Li, Juanfan Wu, Yufeng Wang, Shuxin Zheng, Xiaoqing Zhang
publish: arXiv
abstract: Model routing assigns each query to a suitable foundation model, but tasks and available models keep changing, and existing routers are either untrained for the pool at hand or fit once and forget earlier tasks when updated. We present AdaptRouter, an adaptive router trained by policy learning: a compact multimodal decision model reads each question with cards describing the current experts and learns from native task feedback, without routing labels, to select one frozen expert. Open-weight and API experts share the router, its inputs, and the quality-cost trade-off but use different losses: cheap open-weight experts are explored with RL, whereas paid API experts are queried once and their cached feedback is reused as soft labels. New tasks are learned without replay, new experts enter as cards, and an open-weight quality-first advantage provably keeps cost from overriding quality. Across four task stages, AdaptRouter loses at most 0.4 points on earlier tasks, whereas feedback-trained routers lose up to 7.0, and as its pool grows from three to ten experts, its accuracy rises from 67.2% to 72.1%. On five API models, it exceeds GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra (low) by over 22 points at under a third of their cost.

title: Generation and non-thermal annealing of dislocations and atomic-scale roughness by nonlinear surface acoustic waves
authors: Yuan Xu, Maxim V. Shugaev, Leonid V. Zhigilei
publish: arXiv
abstract: Surface acoustic waves (SAWs) are widely used to probe near-surface material properties and microstructure, but their potential to drive permanent structural modification remains largely unexplored. Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations reveal the mechanisms of defect generation and evolution induced by nonlinear Rayleigh waves in Pt. Strong crystallographic dependence of the nonlinear evolution is observed. SAWs on Pt(111) undergo rapid nonlinear sharpening and shock formation, with localized elastic energy and increasing near-surface stresses, whereas much weaker sharpening on Pt(001) allows dissipation to compete effectively with shock formation. For sufficiently strong SAWs on Pt(111), Shockley partial dislocations are emitted from the surface when the resolved shear stress approaches the theoretical shear strength. The highly localized and rapidly changing stress field at the shock front activates multiple slip systems and promotes crossslip and reactions between Shockley partials, producing complex dislocation structures with sessile stair-rod segments. Subsequent SAW interactions activate dislocation sources on slip systems where the stress is insufficient for homogeneous nucleation, leading, in one case, to sequential emission of Shockley partials and formation of a subsurface twinned domain. Repeated SAW passages progressively reduce dislocation density, demonstrating SAW-driven nonthermal annealing. Dislocation interactions with the free surface generate atomic-scale steps, terraces, and other under-coordinated configurations, providing a microscopic pathway for permanent surface modification that may contribute to the acoustically enhanced catalytic activity observed on Pt surfaces. These results establish nonlinear SAWs as drivers of nonthermal defect generation, restructuring, and annealing, opening opportunities for acoustic processing of near-surface microstructure.

title: Shifting the snow line in protoplanetary disks by planet-induced multiple spiral shocks
authors: Shizu Shimizu, Ryosuke T. Tominaga, Satoshi Okuzumi, Takayuki Muto
publish: arXiv
abstract: The snow line location provides important constraints on rocky planet formation. Recent magnetohydrodynamical simulations suggest that Joule heating associated with gas accretion is so inefficient that the snow line can be located inside 1 au around a solar-type star. This challenges in-situ formation of the terrestrial planets in the solar system unless other internal heating processes are present. Previous studies have proposed that spiral shocks induced by an embedded planet potentially shift the snow line outward. In this study, we investigate the impact of shock heating induced by a giant planet on the location of the snow line in two steps. First, we perform two-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations of a disk with a giant planet to model shock heating rates. We construct an empirical formula for total entropy jumps due to multiple spiral shocks interior to the planetary orbit. Second, we calculate the radial temperature profile based on the thermal balance with the modeled shock heating rates. We find that shock heating can substantially increase the disk temperature in inner regions far from the planet when the planetary mass and disk optical depth are sufficiently high. For example, assuming a fixed surface density profile and an opacity of $κ= 1~\rm cm^2\,g^{-1}$, a planet with one-third of Jupiter's current mass at 5 au can shift the snow line outward beyond 1 au. Our results suggest that the early formation of proto-Jupiter in the solar nebula may have enabled rocky planetesimals and protoplanets to form in the present-day terrestrial planet region without invoking additional water removal processes.

title: AutoSECO: Automated Skill Evolution for Cross-Problem Combinatorial Optimization with General-Purpose LLM Agents
authors: Zirui Zhu, Cong Zhang, Ni Zhang, Kuan Xu, Zhiguang Cao
publish: arXiv
abstract: General-purpose large language model (LLM) agents can develop complete solvers for combinatorial optimization problems. Their specialization, however, often relies on workflows engineered for individual problems, limiting the reuse of development expertise. We propose AutoSECO, an automated skill evolution method that learns reusable solver-development guidance from experience. The challenge is that external evaluation measures the completed solver, while the skill guides decisions during development. AutoSECO connects this feedback to guidance deficiencies by tracing performance shortfalls through solver code and recorded development decisions. Revisions are expressed as general instructions and retained only if a fresh solver developed under the revised skill achieves a lower mean evaluation gap. Evolved solely on the traveling salesperson problem (TSP), the skill guides fresh agents in developing solvers for capacitated vehicle routing, job-shop scheduling, and three-dimensional bin packing without further skill evolution. On TSP, the final mean benchmark gap is 0.52\%, compared with 0.98\% for the skill-evolution baseline SkillOpt. Across all four problems, the evolved skill achieves better aggregate results than no skill guidance, the initial skill, and SkillOpt. The same frozen skill also supports solver development under alternative model--harness configurations. These findings suggest that solver-development experience can be retained as reusable expertise for general-purpose LLM agents.

title: The Riemann Hypothesis for L-Functions of Linearly Constrained Kloosterman Families: Frobenius Polynomials and Intersection Cohomology
authors: Hamed Ebadi
publish: arXiv
abstract: We study Frobenius polynomials attached to linearly constrained Kloosterman families, taking the rank-$r(n)=2^n-\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$, weight-$(n+1)$ sheaf of the author's companion papers as an explicit input. The present contribution is the passage from that sheaf to local characteristic polynomials and the intermediate-extension intersection cohomology on $(\mathbb P^1)^n$. We prove the local reciprocal-root bounds and the degreewise purity of the completed factors; their weights are $n+1+i$ in cohomological degree $i$. Using the imported arithmetic relative-image identification, we construct a reflection pairing and derive the completed functional equation with positive root number. We also give a canonical Frobenius-equivariant splitting of the fibrewise compact-support/parabolic sequence by separation of weights and examine the comparison on open coordinate-zero divisors. The statements do not assume global arithmetic Frobenius semisimplicity or a higher-codimension wild-boundary exchange. An explicit source-and-dependency ledger distinguishes results imported from the companion papers from deductions established here.

title: Free rational curves on singular Fano varieties
authors: Zheng Xu
publish: arXiv
abstract: We prove that every klt Fano variety admits a free rational curve in its smooth locus.

title: Improvements to explicit Burgess-strength bounds for quadratic characters of prime modulus
authors: James Punch
publish: arXiv
abstract: For positive integers $M$ and $N$, consider the character sum $S(M,N)=\sum_{n\in[M,M+N)}χ_p(n)$, where $χ_p$ is the quadratic character modulo $p$. Burgess proved that $S(M,N)\ll N^{1-1/r}p^{\frac{r+1}{4r^2}+\varepsilon}$ for any integer $r\geq 2$ and any real $\varepsilon>0$. This was made explicit by Booker, who showed (under size restrictions on $M$, $N$, $p$ and $r$) that $\lvert S(M,N)\rvert \leq α(r)N^{1-1/r}p^{\frac{r+1}{4r^2}}(β(r)+\log{p})^{1/2r}$, where $α(r)$ and $β(r)$ are given in (Booker, 2006). We show that when $M$ is not too small compared to $N$, we can improve $β(r)$ by a fixed amount. If $M$ is also not too large compared to $N$, we can further improve $β(r)$ by an amount proportional to $\frac{M}{M+N}$.

title: Quark and gluon gravitational form factors of the nucleon at next-to-leading order
authors: Ulaş Özdem
publish: arXiv
abstract: We compute the quark and gluon gravitational form factors $A$, $J$ and $D$ of the nucleon in three-point QCD sum rules at next-to-leading order in $α_s$ for the quark and gluon energy-momentum tensors (EMT), treating both at the same order in the $\overline{\rm MS}$ scheme. The nucleon EMT also tests the method, showing where the sum rules are reliable and why. Protected estimators of $D$ and of the trace form factor $\bar c$ require antisymmetric Borel moments, since none with equal Borel masses alone is protected. The $\mathcal{O}(α_s)$ corrections reduce $A_{\rm tot}$ by $32$--$40\%$, $J_{\rm tot}$ by $22$--$27\%$ and $|D_{\rm tot}|$ by $21$--$27\%$, since the perturbative share of the two-point function is much larger. The total form factors agree with lattice QCD for $1\le Q^2\le2.5$~GeV$^2$. At $Q^2=1.5$~GeV$^2$, $A_{\rm tot}=0.337\pm0.113$, $J_{\rm tot}=0.206\pm0.100$ and $D_{\rm tot}=-0.206\pm0.121$. $D$ is the most reliable result: its correlator is mostly perturbative, and its quark and gluon parts agree with the lattice. In $A$ and $J$, a local gluon-condensate term that does not fall with $Q^2$ is the largest, and their gluon shares are well below the lattice, possibly because the gluon EMT couples at this order only through gluon exchange and the condensate. A working region exists only near $β=1$, and the constant part of transitions cannot be separated within the Borel windows. The individual conservation identities deviate at one point by two standard deviations, consistent with a missing finite term in the $g_{μν}$ structure, and $\bar c$ is therefore given at leading order with condensates.

title: Diffusivity and metric exponents for slightly supercritical percolation in high dimensions
authors: Chenlin Gu, Tom Hutchcroft, Xiaoran Li
publish: arXiv
abstract: It is a classical fact that random walk on the infinite supercritical Bernoulli $p$-percolation cluster on $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ converges to Brownian motion with some diffusivity $σ(p)$, and that the graph metric on the infinite cluster has order $μ(p) \|\cdot\|$ at large scales for some constant $μ(p)$ known as the time constant. We compute the near-critical asymptotics of the two quantities in high dimensions, showing that \begin{align*} σ^2(p) \asymp (p-p_c)^2 \qquad \text{ and } \qquad μ(p) \asymp \frac{1}{\sqrt{p-p_c}} \end{align*} for all $p>p_c$. Our results concerning the diffusivity confirm a conjecture of Biskup (2011). We also compute the asymptotic critical probabilities of slabs in the same regime, showing that $p_c( \mathbb{Z}^{d-1} \times \{0,\ldots,n\}) - p_c(\mathbb{Z}^{d}) \asymp n^{-2}$ as $n\to \infty$.

title: Thermal-Guided Low-Light UAV Image Enhancement: A Reliability-Aware Guidance Network and a Unified Benchmark
authors: Zhicheng Zhao, Yu Wang, Jiangong Xu, Lixiang Xu, Chenglong Li, Jin Tang
publish: arXiv
abstract: Thermal-guided low-light image enhancement (LLIE) is promising for nighttime unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) perception because thermal imagery remains informative under severe visible degradation. However, the degraded visible image serves as both the alignment reference and the enhancement target, making thermal guidance uncertain in its spatial correspondence and local utility under low illumination, sensor differences, and UAV motion. Misaligned or unsuitable thermal cues may introduce artifacts, while spatially varying degradation requires region-specific restoration rather than uniform enhancement. To address these challenges, we propose a Reliability-Aware Multi-Strategy Guidance Network (RMGNet) for thermal-guided UAV LLIE under weak optical-thermal alignment. Its Reliability-Aware Guidance Calibration Module (RAGCM) performs coarse-to-fine displacement estimation and jointly evaluates the reliability of aligned thermal guidance and the usability of degraded visible evidence. Based on calibrated guidance, degradation, and reliability cues, the Multi-Strategy Enhancement Routing Module (MSERM) generates candidates for detail preservation, highlight-protected relighting, and thermal compensation, then spatially routes their contributions. We further construct the UAV weakly aligned Optical-Thermal dataset (UWOT), the largest UAV-oriented benchmark to date for weakly aligned optical-thermal low-light enhancement, containing 5,000 triplets. Extensive experiments show that RMGNet outperforms representative single-modal and multimodal state-of-the-art methods in enhancement quality while retaining competitive computational efficiency and greater robustness to practical cross-modal misalignment. The dataset and code will be publicly available at https://github.com/mmic-lcl/Datasets-and-benchmark-code.

title: A Constructive Lower Bound for the Growth Constant of Ternary Cap Sets
authors: ZeHua Lu
publish: arXiv
abstract: Let $r_3(d)$ denote the maximum size of a cap set in $\mathbb{F}_3^d$. We prove that the exponential growth constant $Λ= \lim_{d\to\infty} r_3(d)^{1/d}$ is strictly greater than $2.22920646813$. The main advance comes from combining two-color recursive synchronization with cross-layer joint filling of a seven-dimensional local alphabet that contains collinear triples (lines). By encoding marked positions as $14$-step closed walks on a two-state directed graph, any zero-sum triple with a fixed outermost color is forced to choose the identical closed walk---and hence the identical record---at every recursive layer, at a net cost of $1000$ dimensions per level. Because the open seven-dimensional coordinates are deferred to the outermost layer, all positions of the same type across all layers can be pooled per record and filled jointly via grouped binary-flag nodes. A $2\times 2$ transfer matrix governs the weighted record count, and spectral dominance over two tilted tail matrices converts this count into a capacity lower bound. Feeding each resulting bound back into the filling parameters iteratively amplifies the growth rate, while a companion-path score exclusion test further enlarges the admissible walk family. The final bound is certified by finite enumeration and exact integer comparisons.

title: STAR: Structure-Aware Temporal Action Recovery for Point Supervised Temporal Action Localization
authors: Yawar Rehman, Min Young Kim
publish: arXiv
abstract: Point supervised temporal action localization is becoming the need of time in this era of ever growing and non-stop video data. Existing method mainly rely on snippet level action response to generate pseudo labels. However, these labels often suffer from boundary ambiguity, over extended proposals, and weak temporal structure. To address these issues, we propose STAR, a structure-aware Temporal Action Recovery framework for point supervised temporal action localization. STAR works by enhancing the base S model with temporal difference interaction with attention module to capture forward and backward snippet changes, and introduces the learning of start, core, and end roles to model the internal temporal structure of actions. In addition, STAR further improves the pseudo label generation through All point proposal ranking and Rolebank based structural re-ranking, which suppress neighbor crossing and structurally inconsistent proposals. Finally, temporal action detector to STAR feedback supervision transfers high quality detector prediction back to the STAR model through soft start, core, end, action, and background targets. This helps to further refine the pseudo labels. Extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks shows the effectiveness of STAR. By using I3D features, STAR achieves 67.2% at AVG@0.1:0.7 on THUMOS'14, 58.1% on GTEA, 74.6% on BEOID, and 31.7% at AVG@0.5:0.95 on ActivityNet-1.3, outperforming previous point supervised methods across multiple benchmarks.

title: PseuDRAGON: Knowledge-Guided Local LLMs for Financial-Data Pseudonymization in Closed Networks
authors: Gwangui Hong, Seonho An, Seonkyu Lim, KyungTae Lim, Min-Soo Kim
publish: arXiv
abstract: Staff pseudonymizing financial data in closed networks must interpret abbreviated column names, identify personal information, and choose processing methods. Local language models can assist, but may give different labels for the same input. PseuDRAGON keeps confirmed judgments and corrections outside a fixed model and reuses them through exact-name lookup and learned rules. For expert review, the workflow searches institutional policy, national privacy law, then international sources. Across 92 columns from one institution, rules increase reuse under the same approval checks from 75 to 83 labels without reuse errors when all training judgments are available. With 25% of the training judgments, withholding non-PII rules for unseen names eliminated the extra PII misses in replay at the cost of lower reuse. Revising or withdrawing approvals rebuilds derived rules, and tests on synthetic records verify that selected methods produce the specified outputs. In three paired runs, the history-first baseline cut automated identification time by 83.0% on average versus no reuse.

title: Toward a Theoretical Understanding of Transformer Attention: Bayesian Estimation and Predictive Sufficiency
authors: Fouad B. Chedid
publish: arXiv
abstract: This paper develops a theoretical account of Transformer attention by organizing existing probabilistic and information-theoretic results. It identifies the assumptions under which attention computes a posterior mean and the additional conditions required for accurate next-token prediction. Posterior-mean optimality under squared-error loss does not by itself establish predictive sufficiency; even a sufficient representation requires a prediction head that uses its information correctly. An excess-log-loss decomposition makes this distinction precise by separating representation information loss from prediction-head error. The analysis clarifies the conditions required for predictive guarantees. Determining when these conditions hold in trained models, and how architectural or training choices can support them, could guide the development of AI systems that preserve and use predictive information more effectively.

title: Stored energy and mechanical load in deformable dielectrics: What the macroscopic fields determine
authors: Bela Schulte Westhoff
publish: arXiv
abstract: The mechanical load that an electric field exerts inside a deformable dielectric has been debated since Kelvin derived it from forces on dipoles and Helmholtz from an energy variation. Current electroelastic models follow the energy route, with the stored energy and its deformation dependence as constitutive input. Using a classical model of ions, electrons, and their fields and spatial averaging, we examine what this energy represents and how much of it the macroscopic fields determine. The macroscopic fields carry only their own energy. In their balance, $\mathbf J_{\rm total}\cdot\mathbf E$ is power leaving them; they do not show where it goes. In the model this power feeds carrier motion and field structure that averaging removes. For linear reversible response its time integral is $\tfrac12\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf P$: $\tfrac12\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D$ is the macroscopic-field energy $\tfrac12\varepsilon_0|\mathbf E|^2$ plus recoverable energy of this structure. Thermal, kinetic, and elastic energies follow likewise, giving one energy map across thermodynamics, mechanics, and electrodynamics. Under deformation the same exchange supplies mechanical work; the fields fix the total, not its division between work and stored energy. We formulate a sufficiency criterion: a macroscopic description determines the load when all microstructures consistent with it give the same virtual work for the deformations of interest. For linear, nonlinear, and hysteretic response we specify the material information required; the linear case recovers the Helmholtz stress. Two dipole arrays with identical macroscopic fields, previously found to differ in boundary traction, show that sufficiency can fail; the criterion separates cases where constitutive data suffice from those needing interface or microstructural detail.

title: Ziv: A Language for Correctly Rounded Math Libraries
authors: Lucas Yunkyu Lee, Sungjin Hwang, Wonyeol Lee
publish: arXiv
abstract: Developing performant, correctly rounded math libraries is challenging. Such implementations often rely on extended-precision arithmetic for correct rounding and precomputed constants for performance. Existing implementation languages, however, provide limited support for (i) high-level abstractions for such arithmetic and (ii) staged computation to combine precomputation and runtime computation in one program. As a result, existing implementations often miss abstraction opportunities and hard-code constants precomputed using separate programs. These practices make it difficult to write, understand, and modify these libraries. We present Ziv, a programming system for developing correctly rounded math libraries. It consists of a small language, a rich standard library, and a provably sound compiler targeting C. Ziv supports (i) high-level numerical abstractions via types and operations for extended-precision numbers, and (ii) staged computation via compile-time evaluation of expressions known to be input-independent. These features enable high-level code that unifies precomputation and runtime computation. We embed Ziv in Julia and evaluate it by reimplementing 19 functions from two state-of-the-art libraries targeting correct rounding; we achieve competitive performance with 2.63$\times$ reductions in lines of code. We also implement three new functions and automatically explore 824,256 variants, achieving 96.5$\times$ average speedup over an arbitrary-precision library.

title: Edge-asymmetric magnetism in semi-Dirac quantum dots
authors: Mustafa Polat
publish: arXiv
abstract: In this study, we investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of quantum dots (QDs) throughout the transition from the Dirac limit to the semi-Dirac limit and beyond. When non-interacting semi-Dirac fermions are confined in triangular QDs, the resulting electronic states near the Fermi level are localized asymmetrically among the three edges of these systems. In the presence of electron interactions, we show that these low-energy states favor the formation of edge-asymmetric magnetism in triangular QDs. In particular, the magnetic moments were localized only along a single edge of the zigzag triangular QDs, corresponding to an edge-asymmetric ferromagnetic ground state. For various system sizes, these zigzag triangular QDs exhibit a one-unit increase in the ground-state total spin ($ΔS_z = +1$) beyond the semi-Dirac limit, revealing a striking result of this transition. In contrast, the remaining two edges are antiferromagnetically coupled in the armchair triangular QDs, indicating an edge-asymmetric antiferromagnetic (AFM) ground state. We further identified the AFM ground states in hexagonal QDs, indicating that these types of asymmetric configurations are not unique to triangular QDs. Collectively, edge-asymmetric magnetism could create potential opportunities for future spintronics.

title: Alpha-points of a putative binary $q$-analog of the Fano plane
authors: Sascha Kurz
publish: arXiv
abstract: A point $P$ of a putative $q$-analog $\mathcal{D}$ of the Fano plane is an $α$-point if the derived design of $\mathcal{D}$ in $P$ is a Desarguesian line spread. Kiermaier showed that for $q$ prime or even every hyperplane contains a point which is not an $α$-point. For $q=2$ we study the $45$ blocks of $\mathcal{D}$ inside a hyperplane $H$. Call a $5$-subspace of $H$ a $β$-flat if all its blocks pass through one point, its focal point. We show that at least $41$ points of $H$ are not focal points of $β$-flats. Consequently $\mathcal{D}$ has at least $85$ non-$α$-points, at most $42$ $α$-points, and at most $22$ $α$-points in every hyperplane.

title: First-Order Entropic Sampling of Words with Prescribed Letter Counts in Linear Time
authors: Olivier Bodini, Francis Durand
publish: arXiv
abstract: We sample, exactly and uniformly, a word of length n over the alphabet {0, . . . , r} in which the letter j occurs a prescribed positive number k j of times, from a source of fair random bits. Every exact sampler reads on average at least H = log 2 (___ n k0,...,kr )___ bits. We give a sampler that reads on average at most H fresh bits, whatever r and the counts, and that performs O(n) bit operations on average over every fixed alphabet, in a bit-RAM in which a memory access costs O(1) while arithmetic is charged bit by bit. Both bounds are optimal: the first one to first order, the second one up to a constant factor, since writing the output already costs $Θ$(n). The sampler writes the word as a Huffman tree of independent binary words, and samples each of them in one of two ways. Binary words with few ones are generated by random insertions; the rank of each inserted letter among its copies, which the Fisher-Yates shuffle generates for nothing, is uniform and independent of the word, and is given back to a recycling source of uniform integers, where it pays for the next insertions. Binary words with many ones are generated by MergeShuffle driven by blocks of $Θ$(log n) bits of entropy; a block is decoded by locating only its ones when the minority letter is rare, and otherwise, its number of ones being concentrated, by a precomputed table of the blocks of typical type, of size O( $\sqrt$ n log 4 n), the rare atypical blocks being decoded slowly.

title: Conservative Rupture Force Relating Co-seismic Rupture and Afterslip Process
authors: Yuxuan Hou, Zeyan Zhao, Han Yue
publish: arXiv
abstract: The post-seismic phase plays a crucial role in the earthquake cycle by releasing co-seismic stress and reshaping the fault-zone stress field. Traditionally, the relationship between afterslip and co-seismic slip is made by the ratio of their respective moment ($R_M$). However, in this study, we perform numerical and theoretical analyses to reveal that $R_M$ is inherently unstable. To quantify the afterslip, we first introduce an inter-seismic "equilibrium state" as a reference from which the pure afterslip is separated, while the afterslip releases the co-seismic stress loading over the velocity-strengthening region after correcting for this equilibrium state. To define the relationship between co- and afterslips, we propose a novel physical quantity termed the "conservative rupture force" (CRF), which is defined as the area integration of co-seismic stress drop. The CRF is equal to the area integration of stress loading over an infinite fault plane as well as the area integration of afterslip stress release over an infinite time and fault plane. This relationship holds for both full-space and half-space faults. We derive a dimensionless parameter as the ratio between afterslip and co-seismic CRFs as $R_F$. We also propose a strategy to derive such a factor with given co-seismic and afterslip models. We demonstrate that after correcting for the spatial partitioning of stress release, $R_F$ converges to one in an infinite time. This strategy is applied to the 2015 Mw 7.8 Gorkha earthquake, and we find that afterslips released 30% of coseismic stress loading over 5.5 years after the mainshock, while a large portion of the fault plane remained locked. The introduction of the equilibrium state and CRF offers a fresh quantitative view to understand relationships between inter-, co- and post-seismic fault slips.

title: Dark matter mass fraction in axion stars
authors: A. S. Dmitriev, D. G. Levkov, A. G. Panin, I. I. Tkachev
publish: arXiv
abstract: QCD axion dark matter is fragmented into small mass miniclusters of high density. With the natural parameters of miniclusters, the time for Bose-Einstein condensation is less than the age of the Universe, which leads to the formation of Bose stars inside these structures. Recently, the problem of the subsequent growth of Bose stars was solved analytically (Dmitriev et al, Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 091001 (2024)). We use this solution to determine present day mass fraction of dark matter in Bose stars and their mass function.

title: Weighted Flow Time Does Not Admit Constant-Competitive Randomized Algorithms
authors: Alexander Lindermayr
publish: arXiv
abstract: We study online preemptive scheduling on a single machine with the objective of minimizing the total weighted flow time. Bansal and Chan (SODA 2009) showed that no deterministic online algorithm is $O(1)$-competitive for this problem. We show that no randomized online algorithm is $O(1)$-competitive against an oblivious adversary either. This settles the remaining case of the long-standing question whether the problem admits an $O(1)$-competitive online algorithm. Quantitatively, every randomized online algorithm has a competitive ratio in $Ω(\min\{\log\log W,\log\log\log\min\{P,D,n\}\})$, where $n$ is the number of jobs and $W$, $P$, and $D$ are the ratios of the largest to the smallest job weight, size, and density (weight divided by size), respectively. The lower bound also holds with high probability, with the same asymptotic dependence on the instance parameters. For every $ρ\ge1$ and every randomized online algorithm, there is an instance on which the cost of the algorithm is at least $ρ$ times the optimal cost with probability at least $1-2^{-2^ρ}$. Both lower bounds hold even if the algorithm knows in advance the size and weight of every job in release order and, for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, every interarrival time up to a factor of $1+\varepsilon$.

title: Video Generalized Category Discovery
authors: Bardia Safaei, Vishal M. Patel
publish: arXiv
abstract: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to categorize unlabeled data from both known and unknown classes using labeled data from only the known classes. While recent GCD methods have shown promise on static images, their performance degrades in videos due to temporal dynamics, larger intra-class variation, and the lack of temporal consistency in existing approaches. We introduce VideoGCD, a framework tailored for video action recognition under the GCD setting. Our method integrates (i) a partitioned Mixture-of-Experts module that encourages specialization for known and novel categories, (ii) a novel-class balancing loss to reduce bias toward known classes, and (iii) a temporal optimal transport loss that promotes consistent routing across frames. Experiments on three video benchmarks demonstrate that VideoGCD significantly improves performance over existing GCD methods, particularly on novel categories. Our findings highlight the importance of combining temporal modeling and expert specialization for video GCD.

title: Spin-controlled thermophase and noise-optimized thermometry in multiorbital quantum dots
authors: Markus Plautz, Jeroen Danon, Jacob Linder
publish: arXiv
abstract: Converting temperature differences into electrical signals underlies both thermoelectric energy conversion and thermometry, which is essential for managing heat in cryogenic quantum technologies. Superconducting circuits typically show a weak thermoelectric response, since their quasiparticle spectrum is nearly particle-hole symmetric. In a Josephson junction, a temperature difference can instead be converted into a superconducting phase difference in an open circuit. We investigate this thermophase effect in a setup where the junction consists of a two-orbital quantum dot with Rashba spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and Zeeman splitting. A second orbital near the superconducting coherence peaks supports quasiparticle transport over a broad gate range. Zeeman splitting can enhance the thermophase by suppressing pair transport, while spin-orbit hybridization shifts the orbital resonances and can reverse the sign of the response. We assess the junction as a phase-based thermometer using a noise budget that includes readout and current noise together with fluctuations of the orbital energies and the magnetic field. The optimal operating points do not maximize the thermophase but balance a large quasiparticle response against sensitivity to parameter fluctuations.
